title: Deals Are Found by Systems, Not by Luck
summary: Good deals rarely arrive on their own; they come from a pipeline fed by brokers, landowners, institutions and your own research, filtered by written criteria. Learn the sources, the stages and the screening rule, and business development becomes a weekly discipline rather than a hope.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the developer who waits for a good deal to be offered will be offered the deals everyone else declined. Business development is the system that puts you in front of the right opportunity early: a set of sources you cultivate, a written test that filters what they send, and a pipeline you review every week.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 73?

A. Treat every safety concern raised by the people who live in, work on or neighbour a building as evidence to be investigated and answered in writing, never as a relationship problem to be managed.

Q. Why is a payment through an agent still the company's risk under modern anti-bribery law?

A. Because those laws commonly reach payments made through intermediaries and hold companies liable for what their agents do on their behalf.

Q. What is a BATNA, and why does it matter in negotiation?

A. Your best alternative to a negotiated agreement: what you will do if this deal fails. It sets how firmly you can hold a position, because the deal only has to beat it.

Why this matters

A developer's returns are set early. The price paid for land, the terms negotiated and the competition faced are mostly decided before any design begins, and the best of those advantages go to whoever saw the opportunity first and was trusted enough to be shown it. That is business development: the work of finding, qualifying and winning opportunities. It is not selling and it is not networking for its own sake. It is a process with inputs, conversion rates and a cost, and you can manage it like one.

This week covers the sources of deals, the pipeline that carries them, the brokers, landowners and institutions you will work with, and the relationships that make you the first call rather than the last. Today is the frame.

The five sources of deals

In plain English: opportunities come from five places, and each needs a different kind of attention.

First, brokers, who represent sellers and sometimes buyers, and whose interest is a commission on a closed transaction. They bring volume and market knowledge, and their best opportunities go to buyers they believe will close. Second, landowners directly: families, farmers, churches, companies with surplus property. Their interest is usually not only price; it can be legacy, timing, tax or a continuing stake. Third, institutions: banks with distressed loans, public bodies disposing of land, pension funds and large owners seeking development partners. Their interest is process and defensibility. Fourth, your own research, finding sites that fit a thesis before anyone markets them. Fifth, your network of past partners, consultants, lenders and contractors, who see opportunities first because they are already working nearby.

A worked example, hypothetical. Over a year, a small developer logs 120 opportunities: 60 from brokers, 20 from direct landowner contact, 10 from institutions, 15 from his own research and 15 from his network. He closes two. One came from his research, a site he identified and approached before it was marketed; the other came from a lender who knew a borrower wanted out. Neither came from the broker volume that took most of his time. That pattern is common, and it is why the source of each deal must be tracked.

The pipeline and its stages

A pipeline is the set of opportunities you are actively considering, organised by stage. A simple version has five stages: identified, screened, under analysis, under offer and closed or dead. Each stage has an exit test. An opportunity moves from identified to screened only if it passes your written criteria. It moves to analysis only if a quick residual calculation, the land value the project can support, shows it is worth more time. It moves to offer only when you know your maximum price and your walk-away terms.

The professional framing for the written criteria is a buy box: the location, size, zoning, price range, asset type and deal structure you pursue, stated in a paragraph a broker can remember. A buy box saves time on both sides. A broker who knows exactly what you buy sends you more of it, and you can decline the rest in a sentence.

The dead stage deserves as much care as the closed one. Every dropped opportunity gets a line in a dead-deal log: the date, the source, the stage it reached and the reason it died, whether price, zoning, title, financing or a better buyer. After a year, that log tells you which sources waste your time, which criteria you keep bending, and where your analysis is too optimistic. It is the cheapest market research you will ever buy, because you have already paid for it in hours.

Say that out loud now.

A written buy box, five stages with exit tests, and a source logged for every deal.

Relationships: being the first call

The developers who see the best opportunities first share three habits. They answer quickly, even when the answer is no. They are clear about what they want, so a broker or a landowner can match them easily. And they close what they say they will close, on the terms they offered, so they are known as reliable. Reliability is the asset. A broker who has seen you retrade, that is, try to cut the agreed price after signing, will not bring you the next good deal first.

A second worked example, hypothetical. Two buyers offer for the same site. One offers 3,100,000 dollars with a 90-day due diligence condition and a history of renegotiating after inspections. The other offers 3,000,000 dollars with 45 days of diligence and a record of closing on agreed terms. A seller and their broker may well take the lower offer, because the expected value of the higher one, discounted by the chance it is cut, is smaller. Your reputation for certainty is worth money at the negotiating table.

How the best do it

Large owners and developers run business development as a formal function: a defined investment thesis, a pipeline reviewed at a weekly meeting, a dead-deal log explaining why each opportunity was dropped, and a relationship plan naming the brokers, owners and institutions each team member is responsible for. A small developer can copy it with one spreadsheet and a 30-minute weekly review.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: pursuit costs on deals that never close may be treated differently from costs on deals that do; verify against the primary source. Liability: letters of intent and confidentiality agreements signed while sourcing can bind you; read them. Banking: lenders are sources of deals as well as funding, and a strong relationship brings both. Governance: decide who may make offers on the company's behalf and up to what price. Estate: relationships with brokers and landowners are personal; document them so the business can continue them. Exit: the brokers who sell to you are the ones who will sell for you.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is activity mistaken for progress: a full pipeline of opportunities that never fit the buy box, absorbing time and pursuit money. The control is a written buy box and an exit test at each stage.

The beginner's mistake

Treating every opportunity as worth analysing. Most should be declined in minutes, politely and quickly, which is itself a service that earns you better opportunities.

Callback

In Week 17, Sage reverse engineered a deal from public information: implied land price, rent and return. That is the analysis stage of the pipeline in miniature. Business development puts that skill to work on many opportunities quickly, so you know within an hour whether a site deserves a week.

Recap

Deals come from brokers, landowners, institutions, research and your network. A pipeline with a written buy box and exit tests filters them, and a reputation for quick answers and reliable closing makes you the first call.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: the full pipeline that closed nothing, a composite.
checklist: I have a written buy box I can state in one paragraph.
I log the source of every opportunity.
I move opportunities between stages only when they pass an exit test.
I decline unsuitable opportunities quickly and politely.
I keep a dead-deal log explaining every drop.
I review the pipeline every week.
I close on the terms I offer and never retrade without a documented reason.
head: Field checklist
speak: Good deals come from systems, not luck. There are five sources: brokers, who bring volume and want a closed commission; landowners directly, who care about more than price; institutions, who care about process; my own research, finding sites before they are marketed; and my network of lenders, consultants and past partners. I log the source of every opportunity, because the best deals often come from the smallest sources. My pipeline has five stages: identified, screened, under analysis, under offer, and closed or dead, and each has an exit test. The first test is a written buy box, my location, size, zoning, price and structure, clear enough for a broker to remember. I answer quickly, even with a no, and I close on the terms I offer. Reliability is the asset: a seller may take a lower offer from a buyer known to close.
terms: Pipeline — the set of opportunities actively under consideration, organised by stage from identified to closed or dead.
Buy box — the written criteria, such as location, size, zoning, price and structure, that define the opportunities a developer pursues.
Retrade — an attempt to reduce an agreed price or change agreed terms after signing, usually after due diligence.

hostile.q: You say you have twenty opportunities in your pipeline. How many will you actually close this year?
hostile.a: On my own history, about one or two. Twenty is the identified stage. Eight passed my buy box, three are under analysis, and one is under offer. My conversion from screened to closed has been roughly one in eight, so I am planning on one close this year and would treat two as a good year. I can show you the dead-deal log for the rest and why each was dropped.

title: The Full Pipeline That Closed Nothing: A Composite
summary: This is a composite example. A young development company built a large pipeline, spent its working capital chasing deals that never fit its strategy, fell into two broker commission disputes, and had no money left when the right deal arrived. Seven forensic steps, with Roman on the cash.
body:
This is a composite example. A developer mistook a busy pipeline for a healthy one, spent his liquidity pursuing deals he should have declined in minutes, and was out of cash, and out of credibility with one broker, when the deal that truly fitted him finally came.

Recall

Q. What is a buy box?

A. The written criteria, such as location, size, zoning, price and structure, that define the opportunities a developer pursues.

Q. What makes a promise to a community safe to make?

A. Measurable terms, a trigger and an end date, a cost already in the pro forma, and a mechanism and consequence behind it.

Q. What is a reservation price in negotiation?

A. The worst terms you will accept before walking away, set in advance from your alternatives, and not disclosed to the other side.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman sits with me because this failure is a liquidity failure wearing a business development costume. Nothing dramatic happens in it. No fraud, no collapse, no headline. A capable developer simply spent eighteen months and most of his free cash being busy. This is a composite, assembled from patterns that recur among small developers, and every number is a hypothetical round figure.

1. Timeline

Month 0: a developer finishes his first small project and sets up a company with 1,000,000 dollars of working capital for the next deals. He tells every broker in the city he is buying. Months 1 to 6: he receives about 90 opportunities, ranging from a corner lot to a hotel, and analyses 30 in detail. Months 4 to 12: he signs letters of intent on six sites, pays for surveys, environmental desk studies and design concepts on each, and posts option fees or deposits on three. Month 9: a broker he had spoken to about a site sends a formal claim for commission after he begins negotiating that site through a second broker. Month 14: four deals have died, for price, zoning, title and financing. His working capital is down to 250,000 dollars. Month 16: a family landowner he met a year earlier, whose site fits his strategy exactly, calls to say they are ready to sell. He needs 300,000 dollars for deposit and diligence within 30 days. He cannot raise it in time, and a competitor signs instead.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions shaped the outcome. Announcing that he would buy almost anything, which filled the pipeline with deals that fitted nobody's strategy. Spending on diligence and design at the letter-of-intent stage for six sites at once, rather than screening hard and committing to one or two. And engaging with a property through a second broker without settling, in writing, who had introduced it.

3. Assumptions

He assumed that more opportunities meant more closings. He assumed pursuit costs were small and recoverable, when most were sunk the moment a deal died. He assumed a conversation with a broker created no obligation. And he assumed the landowner relationship would keep, without any contact in the year between.

4. Incentives

Brokers were paid on closed sales, so they sent him everything; volume cost them nothing and might land a commission. Consultants were paid for each study, so every new site was welcome work. The developer felt progress each time a new letter of intent was signed. Nobody in the system was paid to tell him to stop pursuing a deal, and his own sense of momentum argued against stopping.

Say that out loud now.

A busy pipeline is not a healthy pipeline. A healthy pipeline closes.

5. Warning signs ignored

A conversion rate that never moved: 90 identified, 30 analysed, 6 under offer, none closed. Pursuit spending running ahead of any budget, because there was no budget. A broker's email, in month 3, saying he had registered the client's interest in a site, which went unanswered. And a working capital balance falling month by month without any decision to stop.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was around month 12, when the fourth parallel pursuit took working capital below the amount the right deal would need. Up to then he could have dropped the weaker pursuits, kept a reserve for an opportunity that fitted, and stayed in touch with the landowner. After it, the right deal would need money he no longer had.

7. Root cause

The root cause was the absence of a written buy box and a pursuit budget. Without the first, there was no test to decline deals quickly, so they all consumed time. Without the second, there was no limit on what each pursuit could spend, so the pipeline consumed cash. The broker dispute was a separate, avoidable failure of record-keeping.

Roman's view: the cash arithmetic

Look at where the 750,000 dollars went, hypothetically. On six letters of intent, an average of 60,000 dollars each for surveys, environmental desk studies, legal review and concept design: 360,000 dollars. Option fees and deposits forfeited on two of the three posted: 200,000 dollars. Legal costs and a settlement on the commission dispute: 90,000 dollars. Overhead for 14 months spent mostly on pursuit: 100,000 dollars. Almost all of it sunk, recoverable only if a deal closed. A lender would read the company's balance sheet at month 14 and see a borrower with 250,000 dollars of liquidity and no project, which is why the bridge financing the developer sought for the landowner deal was declined. A pursuit budget set at the start, say 150,000 dollars per deal and 400,000 dollars in total, with a reserve kept for the right opportunity, would have left him able to act.

The same eighteen months, done with discipline

Run the counterfactual, because it shows the rule is practical rather than timid. In month 0 the developer writes a buy box: mid-rise residential, three named neighbourhoods, sites of a given size range, zoning already permitting the use. He sends it to eight brokers and tells them what he does not buy. The 90 opportunities shrink to perhaps 25 that fit, and he declines the rest the same day.

He sets a pursuit budget of 150,000 dollars a deal and 400,000 dollars in total, and ring-fences 400,000 dollars as a reserve. He takes two sites to letter of intent at a time, not six. When a deal dies, he logs why and releases its budget. He answers the broker's registration email and confirms in writing who introduced the site. He calls the family landowner every quarter. In month 16, when the landowner is ready, he has the reserve, the relationship and a clean record with every broker, and he signs.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is running many pursuits in parallel, each individually reasonable, whose combined cost drains the cash the best opportunity will need. The control is Rule 74: a written buy box, a pursuit budget per deal and in total, and a reserve that pursuits may not touch.

The beginner's mistake

Treating a broker's email as noise. A broker who writes that he has registered your interest in a property may be laying the ground for a commission claim. Answer it in writing, the same week, and record who introduced what, when.

Callback

In Week 7, Warrick taught the liquidity floor: the cash you never spend, because without it you cannot act or survive. A company needs the same thing. A pursuit reserve is a liquidity floor for business development, protecting the ability to say yes to the right deal.

Recap

A large pipeline without a buy box consumed time; parallel pursuits without a budget consumed cash; an unanswered broker email became a dispute; and when the right deal came, the money was gone.

Rule 74: Pursue only opportunities that pass a written buy box, set a pursuit budget per deal and in total before spending anything, and record every broker introduction in writing before you engage with the property.

Next: JAX on The Money: what a deal costs to find, and how to price a pipeline.
checklist: I decline opportunities outside my buy box within a day.
I set a pursuit budget per deal and in total before spending anything.
I keep a reserve that pursuit spending may not touch.
I commit to diligence on one or two sites at a time, not six.
I answer every broker registration email in writing the same week.
I record who introduced each property, and when, before engaging.
I keep in touch with promising landowners at least every quarter.
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite example. A developer started with 1,000,000 dollars of working capital and told every broker he was buying. In six months he received about 90 opportunities, analysed 30, and signed letters of intent on six sites, paying for surveys, studies and design on all of them and posting deposits on three. A broker he had ignored claimed commission. Four deals died. By month 14 he had 250,000 dollars left, roughly 750,000 sunk in pursuit costs, forfeited deposits and a settlement. Then the landowner whose site fitted him perfectly called, needing 300,000 dollars in 30 days, and a competitor signed. The root cause was no written buy box and no pursuit budget. Rule 74: pursue only opportunities that pass a written buy box, set a pursuit budget per deal and in total before spending anything, and record every broker introduction in writing before engaging with the property.
terms: Pursuit cost — money spent investigating and negotiating a deal before it closes, mostly sunk if the deal dies.
Broker registration — a broker's written notice that it has introduced a buyer to a property, often the basis of a later commission claim.
Sunk cost — money already spent that cannot be recovered, which should not drive the decision to continue.

hostile.q: Your company has spent three quarters of its capital and closed nothing. Why should I lend you bridge money now?
hostile.a: You should not, on the old approach, and I have changed it. I now work from a written buy box, a pursuit budget of a fixed amount per deal and a reserve that pursuits cannot touch. This opportunity passes the buy box, the seller is ready, and I can show you the residual land value, the diligence plan and the cap on what I will spend before you commit. I am asking you to judge the process I run now, with the deal in front of you, not the one I ran last year.

rule: Rule 74: Pursue only opportunities that pass a written buy box, set a pursuit budget per deal and in total before spending anything, and record every broker introduction in writing before you engage with the property.

title: What a Deal Costs to Find
summary: Every closed deal carries the cost of the deals that died on the way to it. This lesson calculates cost per closed deal, the expected value of a pipeline and the price of a slow answer, with hypothetical round numbers, and shows how sourcing quality moves land cost and returns. Warrick's Wealth Ledger closes.
body:
The true cost of a deal is not the pursuit spending on that deal. It is the pursuit spending on every deal you investigated to find it, plus the overhead of looking. Know that number, and you know whether your sourcing is a business or a hobby.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 74?

A. Pursue only opportunities that pass a written buy box, set a pursuit budget per deal and in total before spending anything, and record every broker introduction in writing before engaging with the property.

Q. What is a severe case, and why do lenders size against it?

A. The specific combination of bad outcomes a project must survive; lenders size against it because their loss comes from the bad case, not the average.

Q. In negotiation, what is a concession pattern, in concept?

A. The size and timing of the moves you make; shrinking concessions signal you are near your limit, while large late ones invite more pressure.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, developers often judge a deal by its own pro forma: land, hard and soft costs, revenue, profit. That is right for the deal and wrong for the business, because the business also paid for every dead deal. If you cannot recover that cost, through fees, through better land prices or through the profit on the deals you close, your business shrinks even when each project looks profitable.

Worked example one: cost per closed deal

Hypothetical round numbers for one year of a small developer's business development.

Step 1, direct pursuit costs on deals that died: 5 deals reached analysis or offer and died, at an average of 40,000 dollars each for surveys, studies, legal review and concept design, which is 200,000 dollars.

Step 2, direct pursuit costs on the deal that closed: 60,000 dollars.

Step 3, overhead: half of the developer's own time and an analyst, valued at a hypothetical 150,000 dollars for the year.

Step 4, add them: 200,000 plus 60,000 plus 150,000 is 410,000 dollars.

Step 5, divide by closings: one closed deal, so the cost to find it was 410,000 dollars.

Now compare with the project. If the closed deal earns a development profit of a hypothetical 2,000,000 dollars, sourcing consumed about a fifth of it. If the profit is 800,000 dollars, sourcing consumed half, and the business is barely paying for its own search.

Say that out loud now.

Every deal I close pays for the deals I did not.

Worked example two: the expected value of a pipeline

A pipeline has a value you can estimate. List each live opportunity with its expected profit if it closes and your honest probability that it will.

Opportunity A, under offer: profit 1,500,000 dollars, probability 40 percent, expected value 600,000 dollars. Opportunity B, under analysis: profit 2,000,000 dollars, probability 15 percent, expected value 300,000 dollars. Opportunity C, screened: profit 1,000,000 dollars, probability 5 percent, expected value 50,000 dollars. Total expected value: 950,000 dollars.

Two lessons. First, almost two thirds of the value sits in the one deal under offer, so that is where your best hours go this month. Second, compare expected value with remaining pursuit cost. If B will cost another 120,000 dollars to take to offer and its expected value is 300,000 dollars, it is worth pursuing; if a new study lowers its probability to 5 percent, its expected value falls to 100,000 dollars and the pursuit no longer pays. That is how you drop a deal without regret: the arithmetic, not the mood.

Worked example three: sourcing quality moves land cost

Where a deal comes from changes what you pay for it. A marketed site, sold through a broker to many bidders, tends to clear near the highest price any bidder will pay. An off-market site, found through research or a relationship, can be bought nearer a fair price because there is no auction.

Hypothetical: a site supports a residual land value of 3,000,000 dollars on your assumptions. In a competitive process, the winning bid might be 2,900,000 dollars, leaving little margin for error. Off-market, after a direct relationship with the owner, you agree 2,600,000 dollars on terms that suit the owner's timing. The 300,000 dollar difference goes straight to profit, and on a project with 4,000,000 dollars of equity it is extra profit equal to 7.5 percent of that equity before anything else changes. That is why research and relationships, though slower, are often the most valuable sources in the log.

The price of a slow answer

Speed has a price too, and it runs both ways. A slow answer to a broker costs you the next opportunity. A slow decision on a good deal costs you the deal. But a rushed offer on an unscreened site costs you diligence money and, if you sign carelessly, credibility when you withdraw. The answer is not speed for its own sake but a fast first screen: a buy box test in minutes and a quick residual within a day, so the slow, expensive work is reserved for the few deals that deserve it.

Recovering the cost: fees, reimbursement and partners

A developer recovers search cost in three ways, all commercial practice rather than any standard, so every term is negotiated. First, through the profit on deals that close, which is why the cost per closed deal must stay well below a typical project profit. Second, through a development fee paid by the project to the developer for its work, often a percentage of cost; investors will want to see that the fee is reasonable for the work done, because Week 38 showed its tax character and its alignment effects. Third, through reimbursement of pursuit costs when partners join: a joint venture agreement can provide that agreed pre-closing costs on this deal are reimbursed at closing, though rarely the cost of the deals that died.

Notice the gap. Partners will usually reimburse the costs of the deal they invest in, but not the cost of your search. That remains yours. It is the strongest argument for a buy box: every dead deal you avoid is money that no partner would ever have repaid.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

On your personal balance sheet, pursuit spending is a risk asset with a high chance of going to zero. Treat it that way. Fund it from capital you can afford to lose, not from your liquidity floor, and cap it as a share of the business's capital. Over a career, your most valuable personal asset in this subject is your reputation as a buyer who closes: it lowers the price you pay and raises the quality of what you are shown, and it compounds.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is judging business development by deals signed rather than by cost per closed deal and expected value. The control is to calculate both every quarter and to drop any pursuit whose remaining cost exceeds its expected value.

The beginner's mistake

Letting sunk pursuit costs justify continuing. Money already spent is gone whatever you decide. Only the remaining cost and the remaining expected value should drive the choice. The second mistake is putting a probability on a deal to justify the work you want to do, rather than the work the evidence supports. Write the probability down before the next study, and compare it afterwards.

Callback

In Week 15, Sage taught levered and unlevered IRR and the traps in each. Cost per closed deal is a trap of the same family at the level of the company: a project can show a strong IRR while the company that produced it earns little, because the IRR ignores the search. Look at both levels.

Recap

Cost per closed deal includes the dead deals and the overhead of looking. A pipeline's expected value tells you where to spend your hours and when to drop a pursuit. Off-market sourcing can lower land cost materially. Fast first screens protect both your time and your money.

Next: LEX on The Rules: broker agreements, commissions, confidentiality and non-circumvention.
checklist: I calculate cost per closed deal every quarter, including dead deals and overhead.
I list each live opportunity with an expected profit and an honest probability.
I spend my best hours on the deal with the largest expected value.
I drop any pursuit whose remaining cost exceeds its remaining expected value.
I never let sunk costs justify continuing a pursuit.
I track whether off-market or marketed deals produce my best margins.
I fund pursuit from capital I can afford to lose, never my liquidity floor.
head: Field checklist
speak: Every deal I close pays for the deals I did not. In a hypothetical year, five dead deals cost 200,000 dollars, the deal that closed cost 60,000 and the overhead of looking was 150,000: 410,000 dollars to find one deal. If that deal earns 2,000,000 dollars, sourcing took a fifth; if it earns 800,000, it took half. A pipeline also has an expected value: profit if it closes times the honest probability, summed across live deals. That shows where my hours belong and when to drop a pursuit: when the remaining cost exceeds the remaining expected value, whatever I have already spent. Sourcing quality moves land cost. An off-market site bought at 2,600,000 dollars instead of 2,900,000 in an auction adds 300,000 to profit, equal to 7.5 percent of 4,000,000 of equity. So I run fast first screens and spend slow money only on deals that deserve it.
terms: Cost per closed deal — total pursuit spending, including dead deals, plus business development overhead, divided by the number of deals closed.
Expected value — the profit an opportunity would earn if it closed, multiplied by the probability that it will.
Off-market deal — an opportunity bought without a public or broker-run sale process, usually through research or a direct relationship.

hostile.q: Your project shows a 20 percent profit on cost. What did it cost your company to find it?
hostile.a: About 410,000 dollars, on a hypothetical year: 200,000 on five deals that died, 60,000 on this one and 150,000 of overhead. Against this project's profit that is about a fifth, which I watch quarterly. I also track cost per closed deal by source, and my off-market deals have cost less to find and been bought nearer fair value, so I am shifting my time toward research and direct owner relationships.

title: Brokers, Commissions and the Paper You Sign While Looking
summary: Business development generates documents before any purchase agreement: broker agreements, registrations, confidentiality agreements, non-circumvention clauses and letters of intent. Each can bind you. This lesson explains, in concept, who a broker works for, when a commission is earned, and which clauses in the early paper carry real obligations.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the first documents in a deal are signed casually and enforced seriously. Before you buy anything, you may already owe a commission, owe confidentiality, have promised not to go around someone and have granted exclusivity, all in paper that felt like courtesy.

Recall

Q. How do you calculate cost per closed deal?

A. Add pursuit spending on every deal, including the dead ones, plus business development overhead, then divide by the number of deals closed.

Q. What is a community benefit agreement, and when is it safe to sign?

A. A contract giving community parties defined benefits in exchange for support; safe only with measurable terms, a trigger, an end date and a cost in the pro forma.

Q. What is anchoring in a negotiation?

A. The effect of a first number on everything that follows; the side that sets a credible first figure often pulls the outcome toward it.

Why this matters

Commission disputes, breached confidentiality agreements and arguments over exclusivity are among the most common legal problems small developers face, and almost all of them start with a document someone did not read or a conversation someone did not record. Everything below is concept. Real estate brokerage, agency and contract law vary by jurisdiction, so verify any rule against the primary source, and take legal advice before signing. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer qualified in the governing law.

Who the broker works for

In plain English: a broker is paid by someone, and works for whoever pays.

The professional framing is agency. A listing broker usually represents the seller under a listing agreement, owing duties to the seller, often including loyalty, care and disclosure, while dealing honestly with you. A buyer's broker, engaged by you, represents you. Some arrangements allow one broker to act for both sides, sometimes called dual agency, usually only with disclosure and consent, and with reduced duties to each. Many places regulate brokers by licence, and an unlicensed person may be unable to recover a commission or may commit an offence by acting as one [unverified — confirm independently].

The practical point: when a seller's broker is friendly, helpful and fast, that is good service, not representation. Anything you tell that broker about your maximum price may reach the seller, and probably should, from the broker's point of view. Keep your reservation price to yourself.

When a commission is earned

Commission terms are contractual and vary, so the agreement controls. Common concepts include a commission payable on completion of a sale, or on introducing a buyer who is ready, willing and able to buy on acceptable terms; a requirement that the broker be the effective or procuring cause of the sale, meaning the introduction actually led to it; and a tail period after a listing ends, during which a sale to a buyer the broker introduced still earns a commission. A registration, a written list of buyers a broker says it introduced, is often how a broker protects itself.

A worked example, hypothetical. Broker A emails you details of an unlisted site and the owner's name, saying the opportunity is introduced on the basis of a 2 percent buyer-side fee. You do not reply. Eight months later, Broker B, engaged by the owner, markets the same site and you buy it for 4,000,000 dollars. Broker A claims 80,000 dollars, saying it introduced you. Whether it is owed depends on the documents, the facts and the law. What is certain is that a written reply eight months earlier, either accepting terms or declining the introduction because you already knew the site, would have settled the question cheaply.

Say that out loud now.

Read every early document as if it will be enforced, and answer every introduction in writing.

The early paper

Four kinds of document arrive before any purchase agreement, and each carries real obligations.

A confidentiality agreement, also called a non-disclosure agreement or NDA, limits how you use and share information about the property or the seller. Read its scope, its duration and whether it forbids contacting tenants, lenders or neighbours, which can block your diligence.

A non-circumvention clause, often inside the NDA, forbids you from dealing directly with the owner, or with parties introduced, so as to avoid paying the person who made the introduction. It can last years and cover related properties. Breaching it can make you liable for the fee you avoided, or more.

An exclusivity provision, often inside a letter of intent, stops the seller negotiating with others for a period while you complete diligence. It is one of the clauses in a letter of intent most likely to be binding even when the rest is expressly not. Week 20 covered how letters of intent split binding from non-binding terms.

A buyer's broker agreement, if you engage one, may itself be exclusive and carry a tail period. Know whether you owe your own broker a fee if you buy a site you found yourself.

A second worked example: the clause that blocked diligence

Hypothetical. You sign a seller's NDA to see a building's rent roll. Clause 4 forbids any contact with tenants, the property manager or the municipality without the seller's written consent. Your diligence plan relied on tenant interviews and a call to the planning department about an open enforcement file. The seller's broker now controls the pace of your diligence. The fix was to negotiate the clause before signing: contact permitted with notice to the seller, or a defined diligence protocol. After signing, you are asking for a favour.

What to put in your own broker agreement

When you engage a buyer's broker, you are the one drafting the obligations, so draft them clearly. Name the territory and the asset type the engagement covers, so a site you find yourself in another neighbourhood is plainly outside it. State whether the engagement is exclusive, and if it is, list the sites you already know about as excluded, with dates. Define when the fee is earned, for example on completion of a purchase of a property the broker first introduced in writing during the term. Set a tail period short enough to be fair and limited to properties named in a written list delivered at the end of the term. Require the broker to disclose any fee it receives from the seller. And give yourself a termination right on notice. Each of these is a commercial term, negotiated, not set by any standard; a lawyer should review the final wording.

Finders, investors and securities

A finder introduces buyers, sellers or investors for a fee. Introducing property is one thing. Introducing investors to your offering, for a fee tied to money raised, can engage securities rules on who may be paid for raising capital, as Week 70 outlined in concept. Never agree a success fee for raising investor money without securities advice.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is the double commission: two brokers each able to argue they introduced the same deal, because nobody recorded who came first. The control is a written introduction log, a reply to every broker email that names a property, and a clause in the purchase agreement in which the seller confirms which broker it engaged and indemnifies you against others.

The beginner's mistake

Signing the seller's standard NDA because everyone signs it. Standard means drafted for the seller. Read the non-circumvention and contact clauses and negotiate them before, not after.

Callback

In Week 20, LEX taught what binds in letters of intent and term sheets. The documents in today's lesson are the same problem earlier in the deal: an NDA or a broker email feels preliminary, but formation, conditions and remedies apply to them just as they apply to a purchase agreement.

Recap

Know whom each broker represents, how and when a commission is earned, and which early clauses bind: confidentiality, non-circumvention, exclusivity and your own broker's terms. Answer every introduction in writing and keep an introduction log.

Next: Sage on The Numbers: reverse engineering how many leads it takes to close two deals a year.
checklist: I confirm in writing whom each broker represents before discussing price.
I never tell a seller's broker my reservation price.
I reply in writing to every broker email that names a property.
I keep an introduction log with dates and sources for every site.
I read the scope, duration, contact and non-circumvention clauses of every NDA before signing.
I know which clauses in a letter of intent are binding, especially exclusivity.
I take securities advice before agreeing any fee tied to money raised.
head: Field checklist
speak: The paper signed while looking for deals is enforced seriously. A listing broker usually represents the seller, so friendly service is not representation, and I never share my reservation price with them. Commission terms are contractual: payable on completion or on producing a ready, willing and able buyer, often requiring the broker to be the effective cause, sometimes with a tail period after a listing ends. An unanswered broker email that names a property can become an 80,000 dollar claim, so I answer every introduction in writing and keep a log. Confidentiality agreements can forbid contact with tenants or authorities and block my diligence, so I negotiate those clauses first. Non-circumvention clauses forbid going around the introducer. Exclusivity is often binding even in a non-binding letter of intent. And any fee tied to money raised from investors needs securities advice before I agree it.
terms: Agency — the legal relationship in which a broker acts for a principal, owing that principal duties such as loyalty and care.
Effective cause — the requirement in many commission arrangements that the broker's introduction actually led to the sale.
Non-circumvention clause — a promise not to deal directly with an introduced party in order to avoid paying the person who made the introduction.

hostile.q: Two brokers say they introduced you to this site. Which one are you paying?
hostile.a: The one our records and the documents support, and I can show you why. My introduction log shows I received the site from Broker B on a stated date, I replied to Broker A in writing declining its introduction because I already had the site, and the seller confirms in the purchase agreement that Broker B is its only engaged broker and indemnifies us against any other claim. If Broker A disputes that, our lawyer will respond on the documents.

title: Reverse Engineering the Pipeline From Two Closed Deals
summary: Week 74 is an even week, so we start from the outcome and work backward. Begin with a goal of two closed deals a year and work back through the conversion rates to how many opportunities you must see each week and what the search will cost; then work back from a target return to the most you can pay for land. Hypothetical round numbers throughout.
body:
A business development plan is a conversion funnel read backward: decide how many deals you will close, divide by the honest odds at each stage, and you learn how many opportunities you must see every week. Do the same from your target return, and you learn the most you may pay before anyone quotes you a price.

Recall

Q. What is a non-circumvention clause?

A. A promise not to deal directly with an introduced party so as to avoid paying the person who made the introduction; it can last years and cover related properties.

Q. What is the expected value of an opportunity?

A. Its profit if it closes multiplied by the honest probability that it will close.

Q. Why should you never reveal your reservation price to a seller's broker?

A. Because the seller's broker represents the seller, and passing your limit on is, from its point of view, doing its job.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, most developers set goals like we want to do more deals this year, which cannot be planned, staffed or funded. A number can. Reverse engineering turns the goal into weekly activity, a pursuit budget and a land-price ceiling, each of which you can check against reality every month. All conversion rates below are hypothetical; replace them with your own after a year of keeping the log.

Worked calculation one: from two closings back to weekly activity

The finished outcome: two closed acquisitions in the next twelve months.

Step 1. Under offer to closed. Of deals where you sign a letter of intent, suppose half close; the rest die in diligence, on price or on financing. To close 2, you need 2 divided by 0.5, which is 4 deals under offer.

Step 2. Analysis to offer. Suppose one in three deals you analyse in detail reaches an offer you are willing to make. To have 4 under offer, you need 4 divided by one third, which is 12 deals analysed.

Step 3. Screened to analysis. Suppose a quarter of deals that pass your buy box survive a quick residual calculation and deserve detailed work. To analyse 12, you need 12 divided by 0.25, which is 48 deals passing the buy box.

Step 4. Identified to screened. Suppose 30 percent of opportunities you see fit your buy box. To screen 48, you need 48 divided by 0.3, which is 160 opportunities identified.

Step 5. Per week. 160 over about 50 working weeks is a little over 3 new opportunities a week.

Two closed deals need roughly 160 opportunities seen, 48 passing the buy box, 12 analysed and 4 under offer, about 3 new opportunities every week.

That weekly number is the useful output. If your sources produce only one opportunity a week that you see at all, your goal is not two deals; it is closer to one, unless you change your sources or your buy box. And if your sources send twenty a week, most of them outside your criteria, the problem is not volume but clarity.

Say that out loud now.

Closings divided by the odds at each stage, back to a weekly number.

Which rate moves the answer most

Now test the funnel the way Roman tests a pro forma: change one input at a time and watch the output.

Raise the buy-box fit from 30 percent to 50 percent, by telling brokers more precisely what you buy. The 48 screened deals now need 48 divided by 0.5, which is 96 opportunities, under 2 a week instead of over 3. That is the effect of clarity alone.

Instead, raise the close rate on offers from one half to two thirds, by offering only after harder screening and by building a reputation for closing on agreed terms. Two closings now need 3 offers, 9 analyses, 36 screened deals and 120 opportunities, and two fewer expensive diligence efforts, which saves about 100,000 dollars.

The lesson is that the cheapest improvements are at the two ends of the funnel: be clear about what you want at the top, and be reliable about closing at the bottom. Effort in the middle, analysing more deals, is the most expensive way to hit the same number.

Worked calculation two: the search budget

Now price the funnel, working back from the same outcome.

Screening costs almost nothing in cash, but time: say 1 hour each for 160 opportunities, 160 hours.

Analysis: a quick residual plus a desk review, a hypothetical 5,000 dollars each in consultants and data for 12 deals, which is 60,000 dollars.

Offer and diligence: surveys, environmental desk studies, legal and concept design, a hypothetical 50,000 dollars for each of 4 deals, which is 200,000 dollars.

Total direct search cost: 260,000 dollars, plus your time, for two closings. Cost per closed deal before overhead: 130,000 dollars.

Test that against the business. If each closed project is expected to earn a hypothetical 1,500,000 dollars of development profit, search consumes under a tenth of it before overhead, which is healthy. If the expected profit is 500,000 dollars, it consumes over a quarter, and you should either raise your buy box toward larger projects or cut diligence costs by screening harder.

Worked calculation three: from target return back to the maximum land price

The second reverse engineering sets your ceiling before a broker quotes a price.

Step 1. Start from value. Suppose the completed project would sell for 24,000,000 dollars, the gross development value.

Step 2. Apply your target. If you require a 20 percent profit on total cost, total cost can be no more than 24,000,000 divided by 1.2, which is 20,000,000 dollars.

Step 3. Subtract everything except land: hard costs 13,000,000 dollars, soft costs 2,600,000 dollars and finance costs 1,400,000 dollars, total 17,000,000 dollars. That leaves 3,000,000 dollars for land including its acquisition costs.

Step 4. Remove acquisition costs. If transfer taxes, legal and other acquisition costs are a hypothetical 5 percent of price, the price is 3,000,000 divided by 1.05, about 2,857,000 dollars.

Step 5. Set the offer range. Your ceiling is about 2,850,000 dollars. Your opening offer sits below it, with room for the concessions Week 66 taught you to plan.

Every input here is an assumption you must test in diligence. But the order matters: the ceiling comes from your return, not from the asking price. A developer who starts from the asking price and adjusts the pro forma until it works has reversed the logic and will overpay.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is conversion rates that are hopes rather than history, which produce a plan that looks achievable and is not. The control is to keep a stage log for a year, replace the assumed rates with your own, and re-run the funnel every quarter.

The beginner's mistake

Starting from the asking price and working forward until the numbers fit. Always work back from value and your required return to a ceiling first; then see whether the asking price is anywhere near it. The second mistake is treating a funnel built on borrowed rates as a forecast. Until you have your own log, call it a plan, label the rates as assumptions, and expect to be wrong in both directions.

Callback

In Week 31, Pax and Cole taught highest and best use and residual land value. Today's third calculation is the same residual, used as a business development tool: you run it in an hour at the screening stage, so that the expensive diligence is spent only on sites whose ceiling is above their likely price.

Recap

Two closings worked back through the odds needed about 160 opportunities, or 3 a week, and about 260,000 dollars of direct search cost. A 24,000,000 dollar project at a 20 percent target supported a land ceiling of about 2,850,000 dollars. The ceiling comes from your return, never from the asking price.

Next: Remi on The Room: the first meeting with a family landowner.
checklist: I set a closing goal and divide back through each stage's conversion rate.
I turn the funnel into a weekly number of opportunities to see.
I price analysis and diligence for the whole funnel, not one deal.
I compare cost per closed deal with expected project profit.
I work back from value and target return to a land price ceiling before any offer.
I remove acquisition costs before setting the ceiling.
I replace assumed conversion rates with my own logged history after a year.
head: Field checklist
speak: Work backward from the outcome. To close two deals in a year, with half of offers closing, one in three analysed deals reaching an offer, a quarter of screened deals worth analysing, and 30 percent of opportunities fitting my buy box, I need 4 offers, 12 analyses, 48 screened deals and about 160 opportunities, a little over 3 a week. Pricing the funnel: 12 analyses at 5,000 dollars and 4 diligence efforts at 50,000 make 260,000 dollars, or 130,000 per closing before overhead, which I test against the profit I expect per project. Then the land ceiling. A project worth 24,000,000 dollars at a 20 percent target on cost allows 20,000,000 of total cost; minus 17,000,000 of hard, soft and finance costs leaves 3,000,000; less 5 percent acquisition costs gives a ceiling of about 2,850,000 dollars. The ceiling comes from my return, never from the asking price.
terms: Conversion rate — the share of opportunities at one pipeline stage that reach the next.
Gross development value — the expected value or sale price of the completed project, the starting point of a residual calculation.
Land price ceiling — the most a developer can pay for land and still meet its required return, derived from value and costs before negotiating.

hostile.q: The seller wants 3,200,000 dollars. Your model works at that price if rents rise 5 percent. Why not pay it?
hostile.a: Because my ceiling comes from my return on today's evidence, not from the rent I need to justify the price. On current rents the land supports about 2,850,000 dollars at our target. If the seller will not come near that, the site is not our deal at this time, and I would rather keep the relationship and tell them where we would be than overpay and hope the market rescues us.

title: The First Meeting With a Family Landowner
summary: A hypothetical first meeting with three siblings who inherited a well-located site and have not decided whether to sell. The lesson gives the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the question, when to stay silent and how to hold your state, and closes with a note on personal brand.
body:
A first meeting with a landowner is not a negotiation. It is the start of a relationship in which you learn what the owners actually want, show that you can be trusted with their family's most important asset, and leave without asking for anything except permission to come back.

Recall

Q. How many opportunities must you see to close two deals a year, on the hypothetical rates from Day 5?

A. About 160, or a little over 3 a week, working back through 4 offers, 12 analyses and 48 deals passing the buy box.

Q. What is effective cause in a broker commission arrangement?

A. The requirement, common in many arrangements, that the broker's introduction actually led to the sale before a commission is earned.

Q. Why might a seller accept a lower offer from a different buyer?

A. Because a buyer known to close on agreed terms offers more certainty, and a higher offer discounted by the chance it is cut can be worth less.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the scene is hypothetical. Three siblings inherited a two-acre site on a main road from their father. The eldest wants to sell; the middle sibling wants to keep it for the family; the youngest lives abroad and wants whatever is fair. Their mother, who still lives in a house at the back of the site, has not been asked. You were introduced by their accountant. You are meeting at the mother's house on a Sunday afternoon. Nobody has said the word price yet.

The question behind the question

Each sibling's question has another underneath. The eldest's question, what would you pay, really asks: can you take this decision off my shoulders? The middle sibling's question, why should we sell to a developer, asks: will you respect what our father built? The youngest asks: will I be treated fairly from abroad? And the mother, who says little, may be asking the most important question in the room: where will I live? A deal that answers all four is often worth more to the family than a higher price that answers one.

The lines to say

  • Thank you for having me in your home. I am not here to make an offer today. I am here to understand what matters to your family about this land.
  • Tell me about your father and how he came to own it.
  • There are several ways families do this: an outright sale, a sale over time, a joint venture where the family keeps a share, or keeping the land and leasing part of it. Each suits different goals, and each has tax and legal consequences you should take your own advice on.
  • Whatever you decide, I would suggest each of you has your own adviser, so that nobody feels the decision was made for them.
  • May I come back in a month with some options, after you have talked among yourselves?

Say that out loud now.

I am not here to make an offer. I am here to understand what matters to your family.

The lines never to say

  • I can give you a great price if you move quickly. Urgency in a family decision reads as pressure, and pressure splits families.
  • Your brother says you want to sell. Never carry one sibling's view to another; you will be blamed for both.
  • The land is not worth what you think. You may be right, but the first meeting is the wrong moment, and the second sentence of that kind ends the relationship.
  • We can sort the tax out later. Tax may shape the whole structure, and it is theirs to take advice on, not yours to dismiss.
  • Anything about the mother's house as if it were part of the site. Ask about it as her home.

When to stay silent

Stay silent after you ask about their father. The story will tell you what the land means to them, and families rarely tell it to someone who interrupts. Stay silent when the siblings disagree in front of you; do not take a side, and do not fill the pause with a proposal. And when the mother finally speaks, stop everything else. In many family decisions, the person who has said least holds the deciding vote.

A worked example: options instead of a number

On your second visit you bring three options, each in plain words with hypothetical round numbers, and you ask them to review the options with their own advisers before discussing any of them with you.

Option one: an outright sale at a price within a range your residual supports, say 2,400,000 to 2,700,000 dollars, with a long closing so the mother can arrange a move. Option two: a sale of the front portion only, keeping the mother's house and a garden with the family, which lowers your land cost and keeps her where she is. Option three: a joint venture in which the family contributes the land for a share of the project's profit, more value if the project succeeds and more risk if it does not.

Notice that option two might be the one that unlocks the deal. It costs you some site area and gains you the middle sibling's and the mother's support. Week 33 covered how to value contributed land in a joint venture; today the point is that the structure can answer questions a price cannot.

How to hold your state

Family meetings can feel slow and emotional, and your instinct may be to speed them up. Before you knock, while you are parked, take a couple of slow breaths with a longer exhale, a practitioner habit for settling; check that with your doctor if it is new to you. Inside, match the pace of the room, accept the tea, and expect the business part to take a small fraction of the time. Your composure is information to them: a developer who is patient on the first Sunday is one they can imagine being patient through a two-year closing.

Personal brand

In business development your personal brand is not a logo or a social media presence. It is what an accountant says about you when a family asks who they should talk to. It is built from three things you can control: you answer quickly and honestly, including when the answer is no; you do what you say on the date you said; and you never let one party's confidence reach another.

Ask yourself what you want an introducer to say about you in one sentence, then ask whether your last ten conversations would support it. Write that sentence down. It is your standard, and the gap between it and your record is your work.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is pushing for a commitment before the family has agreed among itself, which forces the disagreement into the open with you at the centre of it. The control is to ask for nothing on the first visit except permission to return, and to insist each sibling takes independent advice.

The beginner's mistake

Leading with a number. A number gives the family something to argue about and you nothing to learn from. Lead with questions, and bring options on the second visit. The second mistake is forgetting the introducer. Thank the accountant afterwards, tell them the meeting happened, and never surprise them with what you propose next.

Callback

In Week 66, Kema and JAX separated interests from positions. Here the position is a price and the interests are a mother's home, a father's legacy and a fair share for a sibling abroad. The developer who negotiates interests can often agree a lower price that leaves the family better off.

Recap

Listen first, answer the question underneath, never carry views between siblings, insist on independent advice, bring options rather than a number, and ask only for permission to return. Your reputation for patience and discretion is the business development asset.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap for business development.
checklist: I ask for nothing on a first visit except permission to return.
I learn the history of the land before discussing its value.
I never carry one family member's view to another.
I recommend independent advice for each owner.
I bring structured options, not a single number, to the second meeting.
I treat any home on the site as someone's home, not part of the lot.
I write down the one sentence I want introducers to say about me.
head: Field checklist
speak: A first meeting with a family landowner is the start of a relationship, not a negotiation. In a hypothetical case, three siblings inherited a site and their mother still lives on it. The eldest wants to sell, the middle wants to keep it, the youngest abroad wants fairness, and the mother may be asking the most important question: where will I live. So I say I am not here to make an offer, I am here to understand what matters to the family. I ask about their father and stay silent while they tell the story. I never push for speed, never carry one sibling's view to another, never dismiss tax, and never treat the mother's house as part of the lot. I insist each owner takes independent advice. On the second visit I bring options: a sale with a long closing, a sale of the front portion keeping her home, or a joint venture. A structure can answer questions a price cannot.
terms: Interests and positions — a position is what a party asks for; an interest is the underlying need that makes them ask for it.
Contributed land — land put into a joint venture by its owner in exchange for a share of the project rather than a cash price.
Personal brand — in business development, the reputation others repeat about you, built from responsiveness, reliability and discretion.

hostile.q: Another developer has offered us 2,800,000 dollars cash. Why should we keep talking to you?
hostile.a: You should consider that offer seriously, with your own advisers. I cannot tell you it is wrong. What I can offer is a different shape of deal: a sale of the front portion that keeps your mother's home, or a joint venture that shares the project's upside, and a record of closing on the terms I agree. If a clean sale at that price is what your family wants, take it. If what matters is more than the number, I would like to show you the options side by side.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 74 Review: Finding Deals on Purpose
summary: Six questions test the week: deal sources, the buy box, Rule 74, cost per closed deal, broker introductions and the land price ceiling. A Red Pen drill finds the defects in a hypothetical monthly pipeline report, and a two-minute boardroom drill closes the week.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: decide in writing what you buy, see enough of it to close your target, spend on the few deals that deserve it, record every introduction, and be the buyer people trust to close.

Recall

Q. What is the question behind an eldest sibling's question, what would you pay?

A. Often: can you take this decision off my shoulders? Answering that, with patience and options, matters more than a first number.

Q. What is Rule 73?

A. Treat every safety concern raised by the people who live in, work on or neighbour a building as evidence to be investigated and answered in writing.

Q. What is a reservation price?

A. The worst terms you will accept before walking away, set in advance from your alternatives and never disclosed.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, business development is where your company's future projects are decided, usually long before anyone else notices. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer. Then do the Red Pen as if a lender had sent you the document and asked whether to believe it.

As you check your answers, notice how many of them are about records rather than relationships: the source log, the dead-deal log, the introduction log, the pursuit budget. Relationships open the door. Records are what let you walk through it without a dispute.

The six questions

Question 1. What are the five sources of deals?

Answer: Brokers, landowners directly, institutions, your own research and your network of past partners, lenders and consultants. Log the source of every opportunity, because the best often come from the smallest sources.

Question 2. What is a buy box, and why write it down?

Answer: The written criteria, such as location, size, zoning, price and structure, that define what you pursue. Written down, it lets brokers send you the right deals and lets you decline the rest in minutes.

Question 3. What is Rule 74?

Answer: Pursue only opportunities that pass a written buy box, set a pursuit budget per deal and in total before spending anything, and record every broker introduction in writing before engaging with the property.

Question 4. How do you calculate cost per closed deal?

Answer: Add pursuit spending on every deal, including the dead ones, plus business development overhead, and divide by the number of deals closed.

Question 5. Why must every broker email naming a property be answered in writing?

Answer: Because it may be a registration that grounds a commission claim; a written reply, accepting terms or declining the introduction, settles who introduced what and when.

Question 6. How do you set a land price ceiling?

Answer: Start from gross development value, divide by one plus your target profit on cost to get maximum total cost, subtract hard, soft and finance costs, then remove acquisition costs. The ceiling comes from your return, never the asking price.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Remi framed deal sourcing as a system: five sources, a pipeline with exit tests and a written buy box. Ford and Roman took a composite developer whose full pipeline closed nothing, giving Rule 74. JAX priced the search: cost per closed deal, the expected value of a pipeline and the land-cost advantage of off-market deals. LEX explained brokers, commissions and the early paper that binds. Sage reverse engineered the funnel from two closings and the land ceiling from a target return. Remi ran the first meeting with a family landowner.

Red Pen

Here is a hypothetical monthly pipeline report a business development manager sent to the company's board. Find the defects before reading on.

Pipeline report, month 6. We now have 42 opportunities in the pipeline, up from 25, a strong month. Total pipeline value is 63,000,000 dollars of profit. We have signed letters of intent on five sites and commissioned surveys and concept design on all five; costs are being tracked by the consultants. Broker C has written about the Main Street site, but we found it ourselves so no reply is needed. On the Riverside site, the asking price is 3,400,000 dollars; we have adjusted rent assumptions so the model works at that price. Dead deals: several, no issues to report.

The defects. First, the pipeline is measured by count, which rewards volume and says nothing about fit with the buy box or progress through the stages. Second, total pipeline value adds the full profit of every deal as if all will close; the honest figure is expected value, each profit times its probability, and it will be a small fraction of 63,000,000 dollars. Third, five letters of intent with paid diligence on all five breaks the discipline of committing to one or two at a time, and there is no pursuit budget or total stated. Fourth, costs tracked by the consultants means the company is not tracking its own spending. Fifth, Broker C's email is exactly the kind that grounds a commission claim; it needs a written reply now, with evidence of when the company found the site. Sixth, adjusting rents until the model works at the asking price reverses the logic; the ceiling should come from value and target return. Seventh, a dead-deal line of several, no issues throws away the log that would show which sources and criteria are failing.

A corrected report would show the funnel by stage with conversion rates, expected value rather than headline profit, pursuit spending against a stated budget, an introduction log with Broker C answered, the Riverside ceiling calculated from value and return, and one line on every dead deal saying why it died.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a new investor who asks, how do you find your deals? Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "We decide in writing what we buy: location, size, zoning, price and structure, and every broker and contact we work with knows it. That lets us decline most opportunities the same day. We need to see about three opportunities a week to close two deals a year, so we track every source, and our best deals have come from our own research and direct relationships with owners, where we pay closer to fair value. We set our maximum land price from the finished value and our required return before anyone quotes a price. We cap what we spend pursuing each deal and in total, keep a reserve for the right one, record every broker introduction in writing, and log why every dead deal died. And we close on the terms we offer, because a reputation for closing is what gets us shown the good deals first."

Score yourself. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you mention the buy box, the ceiling and the pursuit budget? Did you say why reliability matters? Did you finish inside two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a pipeline reported by size, which makes the company look busy while it spends cash and closes nothing. The control is to report by stage, by expected value and against a pursuit budget.

The beginner's mistake

Measuring business development by meetings held and letters of intent signed. The only outcome that counts is a deal closed at or below its ceiling.

Callback

In Week 2, Kema taught the decision journal. The dead-deal log is a decision journal for business development: what you believed when you pursued each deal, and what actually killed it. Reviewed once a year, it corrects your conversion rates and your optimism.

Recap

Five sources, a written buy box and a staged pipeline; cost per closed deal and expected value; brokers, commissions and the early paper that binds; a funnel worked back to a weekly number; a land ceiling worked back from your return; and the patience of a first meeting with an owner. Rule 74 keeps the search affordable.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: governance capture, related-party dealing and handshake deals.
checklist: What are the five sources of deals?
What is a buy box, and why write it down?
What is Rule 74?
How do you calculate cost per closed deal?
Why must every broker email naming a property be answered in writing?
How do you set a land price ceiling?
head: The six questions
speak: I find deals on purpose. Five sources feed my pipeline: brokers, landowners, institutions, my own research and my network, and I log the source of every opportunity. A written buy box tells everyone what I buy and lets me decline the rest the same day. Working back from two closings a year through honest conversion rates, I need about three new opportunities a week. Every closing pays for the dead deals and the overhead of looking, so I track cost per closed deal and the expected value of the pipeline, not its headline size. I set my land price ceiling from finished value and target return before anyone quotes a price. I answer every broker introduction in writing and keep an introduction log. And Rule 74: pursue only what passes the buy box, set a pursuit budget per deal and in total before spending, and record every broker introduction before engaging with the property.
terms: Pipeline report — a periodic summary of opportunities, best shown by stage, conversion and expected value rather than by count.
Introduction log — a dated record of who introduced each property and when, used to settle commission claims.
Dead-deal log — a record of every dropped opportunity and why it died, used to correct sources, criteria and assumptions.

hostile.q: Your report says the pipeline holds 63,000,000 dollars of profit. How much of that do you actually expect to earn?
hostile.a: Far less, and the 63,000,000 figure should not have been reported that way. It adds the full profit of every opportunity as if all will close. On honest probabilities by stage, the expected value is a small fraction of it, concentrated in the one or two deals under offer. I will resend the report by stage, with expected value, pursuit spending against budget and the reasons each dead deal died.
